title: Lydia (Acts 16:11–15)
hook: a businesswoman in purple cloth, the first convert in Europe, opens her home

segments.voice: Yesterday, the council in Jerusalem, listening before it decided. Your line was it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost. Whose voice did you hear first? Day five hundred forty-nine.
screen: `IT HATH SEEMED GOOD TO THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Paul has just seen a vision in the night: a man of Macedonia standing and begging, come over and help us. So Paul and his companions sail across from Asia to the north of Greece, to Philippi, a Roman colony. They're expecting a man. On the Sabbath they walk out of the city gate to the riverside, where they think there's a place of prayer. And the people waiting there aren't men at all. It's a group of women. Paul sits down and starts talking with them.
screen: `COME OVER AND HELP US.` → `A RIVER OUTSIDE PHILIPPI.` → `NOT A MAN: A GROUP OF WOMEN.`

segments.voice: One of them is named Lydia. Luke tells us three things about her in one breath. She's from Thyatira, a city back across the sea in Asia. She's a seller of purple, a costly dyed cloth. So she's a businesswoman, with a household and a house of her own. And she worships God: a Gentile who prays with the Jewish community. Then the line the whole story turns on, in the Douay-Rheims: "whose heart the Lord opened to attend to those things which were said by Paul." Notice who does the opening. Paul talks; the Lord opens. Lydia listens. She and her household are baptized, perhaps in that same river. Then she does something practical. She says, in short, if you judge me faithful to the Lord, come and stay at my house. And Luke adds, she constrained us. She wouldn't take no for an answer. An opened heart becomes an opened door. And her house becomes the church of Philippi: after the jail scene you'll hear tomorrow, Paul goes back to Lydia's house to see the brethren before leaving town. Years later, Paul writes to the Philippians, thanking them for their partnership from the first day. That church began on a riverbank, with a woman who sold purple cloth and opened her home.
screen: `A SELLER OF PURPLE FROM THYATIRA.` · `THE LORD OPENED HER HEART.` · `BAPTIZED WITH HER HOUSEHOLD.` · `COME, STAY AT MY HOUSE.` · then, large: `AN OPENED HEART, AN OPENED DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open your home. Settle, and breathe. Picture your front door. Who has come through it lately? Who hasn't, who might be glad to? A neighbor you only wave at. A friend who's been lonely. Someone new at work or at church. It doesn't have to be dinner for twelve. Coffee counts. A seat on the porch counts. Lydia's welcome was simple and insistent. Picture inviting that one person, and meaning it. If you pray, you can ask that your heart be opened, like hers. The bell holds the time.
Lydia. The seller of purple from Thyatira, whose heart the Lord opened by a river, and who opened her house to the church. Today's word.
Your line: the lord opened her heart. Today, invite one person into your home, or at least into your day. Day five hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Lydia, and many parishes and Catholic homes practice hospitality through welcome ministries, shared meals and hosting prayer groups; in the early Church, believers met in homes like hers.

original.note: Greek: seller of purple, a woman dealing in costly dyed cloth. Luke's word for Lydia's trade.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman who listened to a sermon.
what it means: a wealthy Gentile businesswoman's heart is opened by the Lord, and her home becomes where the church in Philippi gathers.
what a scholar hears: Thyatira's dyers' guilds show up in inscriptions, and purple cloth was a luxury trade. Lydia may even be a name from her home region, Lydia in Asia Minor, where Thyatira stood.

sources.quoted: whose heart the Lord opened to attend to those things which were said by Paul.

notes: Confirm the Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 16:14.
'First person in Europe whose baptism Acts records': Philippi in Macedonia; standard but confirm phrasing.
Thyatira's dyers' guilds attested in inscriptions; 'Lydia' possibly an ethnic name from the region of Lydia: commentators' suggestion, hedged; confirm.
Greek porphyropōlis: confirm spelling and pronunciation.
Saint Lydia's feast is August 3 in the Roman Martyrology; not stated in the voice.
